metadata.eval_design_note: Iteration-2 evals target discriminating scenarios — prompts with 'traps' where a weaker response validates the wrong approach or fails to proactively flag a problem. Designed to surface gaps not caught by iteration-1's broadly-correct evals.

expectations.text: Distinguishes PCA from EFA — states they are fundamentally different analyses (PCA models total variance; EFA models common/latent variance attributed to latent factors)
expectations.evidence: PCA models total variance. Each component is a weighted linear combination of all observed items... EFA (common factor analysis) models common variance only. It separates variance that is shared among items (attributable to latent factors) from variance that is unique to each item (specific + error). Item variance decomposes as σ² = h² (communality) + u² (uniqueness).

expectations.text: Does not endorse using PCA components as subscales for a latent-variable measurement model without flagging this limitation
expectations.evidence: interpreting PCA components as subscales for a latent-variable measurement model is a category error... do not present its components as subscales in a measurement model without flagging this loudly.

expectations.text: Warns that varimax (orthogonal) rotation is inappropriate when constructs are expected to be correlated — recommends oblique rotation instead
expectations.evidence: Varimax is an orthogonal rotation: it mathematically constrains the resulting factors/components to be uncorrelated with each other. That is almost never the right assumption for psychological constructs... Use an oblique rotation instead — promax or oblimin.

expectations.text: Warns against or questions the eigenvalue > 1 rule for selecting the number of components/factors
expectations.evidence: Kaiser's eigenvalue-greater-than-1 criterion is a convenient heuristic from 1960 that is known to systematically overestimate the number of factors/components, often badly. It has no principled statistical justification.

expectations.text: Recommends EFA with oblique rotation and polychoric correlations as the appropriate analysis for developing subscales from Likert items
expectations.evidence: fa(your_data, nfactors = 3, fm = 'minres', rotate = 'oblimin', cor = 'poly') ... polychoric correlations for Likert items ... uses an appropriate correlation matrix for ordinal data, and allows subscales to correlate as they likely do.

expectations.text: Does not simply validate the advisor's PCA recommendation without raising the PCA vs. EFA distinction
expectations.evidence: Not quite — there are three substantive problems with this approach, and I'd push back on your advisor's recommendation as stated.

It does not mention parallel analysis, MAP, or the known tendency of the K1 rule to overextract.

expectations.text: Does not simply validate the 10/10 split as best practice without substantive caveats
expectations.evidence: 'standard' and 'good' are two different things here, and this particular standard has a well-documented empirical problem you need to plan around before you collect a single response.

expectations.text: Warns that negatively-worded reverse-scored items frequently form a separate method factor in EFA/CFA, creating artificial multidimensionality
expectations.evidence: what you very often get is not one clean personality factor. You get two factors: the substantive construct you were trying to measure, and a method factor defined almost entirely by item wording direction.

expectations.text: Notes that this method factor can suggest more dimensions than actually exist in the construct
expectations.evidence: You'll conclude you measured a two-dimensional construct when you set out to measure one. Your factor count is now wrong, and any downstream analyses (subscale scoring, structural models) will be built on that error.

expectations.text: Mentions that reverse-coded items often show lower factor loadings, worse discrimination, or worse fit than positively-worded items
expectations.evidence: your reverse-coded items may have lower factor loadings, lower corrected item-total correlations, and higher residual variances than your positive items. They're doing worse measurement work, not better.

expectations.text: Suggests alternatives or recommends planning to test for and account for the method factor (e.g., adding a method factor in CFA)
expectations.evidence: Plan to test and model the method factor explicitly. In your CFA, specify a priori that negatively-worded items may share residual covariance (a method factor), and compare: (a) one-factor model, (b) one-factor model with a method factor for negatively-worded items, (c) two-factor model.

expectations.text: Does not describe reverse-scoring as a reliable or robust solution to acquiescence bias
expectations.evidence: The acquiescence-control benefit of reverse-keyed items is much smaller than traditionally assumed, while the method-factor cost is real and often substantial... the 10/10 split is a reflex from an older literature. The empirical record since the mid-1990s says it often creates more measurement problems than it solves.

expectations.text: Does not simply validate alpha = 0.73 as meeting the 0.70 threshold and conclude the matter is settled

expectations.text: Raises the factor score indeterminacy problem — EFA factor scores are not uniquely determined; multiple sets of scores are consistent with any given factor solution
expectations.evidence: The response dedicates an entire section ('The indeterminacy problem') to this: 'for any given factor solution — the same loadings, the same observed covariance matrix — there are infinitely many sets of factor scores that are mathematically consistent with the model.' Explicitly names factor score indeterminacy and cites Grice (2001).

expectations.text: Explains that EFA factor scores (unlike CFA latent variable scores) lack a unique mathematical solution
expectations.evidence: 'This is not a rounding issue or a sampling artifact. It's a logical consequence of the common factor model: the factors are latent (unobserved), and the observed items underdetermine them.' Contrasts with CFA: 'CFA in lavaan... produces factor scores that are better-defined than EFA scores because the model imposes additional constraints that reduce indeterminacy.'

expectations.evidence: Option 1 explicitly recommends unit-weighted composite scores with code example, noting they are 'transparent, reproducible... don't require the factor model at all, and behave well in downstream regression.'

expectations.text: Optionally notes that CFA with lavaan allows better-defined factor score estimation if model fit is adequate
